subject: Chemistry
title: Alchemical Symbols and Secret Codes
description: A micro-lesson that makes Alchemical Symbols and Secret Codes usable.

hook.text: Alchemists wrote in code—using symbols for elements, planets for metals, and dragons for chemical reactions.

buildup.text: Gold was the Sun (☉), silver was the Moon (☽), copper was Venus (♀), and iron was Mars (♂).

discovery.text: They encoded recipes in allegorical images: a green lion eating the sun meant acid dissolving gold.

twist.text: The secrecy was deliberate. Alchemists feared persecution—and wanted to keep profitable secrets from competitors.

climax.text: Modern chemists still use some alchemical symbols. ♀ and ♂ for copper and iron became the symbols for female and male.

punchline.text: Planets for metals, dragons for reactions. Chemistry's first language was art.

quiz.question: In alchemical symbolism, what did a green lion eating the sun represent?

details.summary: Alchemists developed an elaborate system of symbols to represent elements, compounds, and processes. Planets represented metals (gold was the Sun, silver was the Moon, mercury was Mercury), while processes like distillation, calcination.
details.whyItMatters: Alchemical symbols were the predecessors of modern chemical notation and element symbols. The tradition of symbolic representation in science evolved directly from alchemical encoding practices.
takeaways: Planetary symbols represented the seven known metals in alchemical texts
Secrecy protected valuable knowledge and prevented dangerous misuse
Modern chemical symbols evolved from alchemical symbolic traditions

faq.question: Why did alchemists write in codes and symbols instead of plain language?
faq.answer: Secrecy served multiple purposes: protecting valuable trade knowledge from competitors, preventing dangerous processes from being replicated by the unskilled, maintaining mystical authority, and avoiding persecution by religious and political authorities who viewed alchemy with suspicion.

faq.question: How did alchemical symbols evolve into modern chemical notation?
faq.answer: John Dalton first proposed using circles with letters for elements in 1803. Jöns Jacob Berzelius simplified this to letter abbreviations in 1813, creating the system we still use..
